turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Seán. Come on through, the doctor's free now. I've already dipped the urine.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, thanks. I'm, uh, a bit shook, to be honest.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He wouldn't stay in the bed at all.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sit yourself down there. What's been going on with you?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the pain, doctor. A fierce pain in my left side since around three this morning, going down into the groin. Came on all of a sudden.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that sounds rotten. When did you first notice it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): In the night, like I said. Uh, I woke with it around three.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I heard him pacing at half three. I was in the spare room.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is it still on you now?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It is, yeah. If I move about it eases a small bit, then it grabs me again. I'd say a seven, umm, maybe an eight. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Did your stomach turn with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I vomited the once, in the night. Nothing since. Just that once.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And when I went into the loo after him, there was blood.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. The wee was pink in the night, and it's still a bit pink this morning.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any burning or stinging when you pass water?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No burning.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish, or had the shakes?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I haven't.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your breathing? Any cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's grand. No bother there.
[SEG0021] person_1 (NURSE): Will I give you the dip? Blood three plus, protein a trace, leucocytes negative, nitrites negative.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. What about his numbers?
[SEG0023] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 96, temperature 36.7. He's a bit sweaty, but he's chatting away grand.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. Can I have a feel of your tummy?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, go on.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Left loin is sore when I press. Tummy is soft, no guarding, and the right side is quiet.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah, that's the place.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at home, medicine-wise?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, amlodopine, five milligrams, one in the morning, for the pressure.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): And the cholesterol one at night, the little white tablet, twenty milligrams, for the cholesterol. I don't know the name of it, doctor.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet as well, two and a half milligrams, mornings.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the ayurvedic powder in the morning too, a teaspoon, from the health shop. That's all, I think.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and I took two Nurofen around six, for this pain. Didn't touch it, really.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The morning was mad. I was late with my husband's metformin, and I nearly forgot my own aspirin, the one for my heart.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): My sister in Galway had a stone years back. She's flying now, but that's her, not him.

[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): What happens is a little stone can sit in the tube from the kidney to the bladder. The kidney swells a bit trying to push the urine past, and that sends the pain down into the groin.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Is that, umm, dangerous? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting the pain down into the groin, the blood in the urine, and that dip together, my working impression is a ureteric stone, renal colic.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll book a CT of the kidneys for this afternoon, to see if there's a stone.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): And for the pain I'll start diclofenac, fifty milligrams by mouth, three times a day. First dose at lunchtime, seeing as you had the Nurofen at six.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Do I leave the Nurofen off, then?

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, no more Nurofen while you're on the diclofenac. Drink plenty of water. If you get a fever, or you can't pass urine, or the pain gets unbearable, come straight back in.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stay with him. I do his mornings, I'm the carer.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll see you back here this afternoon, after the scan, and I'll go through it with you.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so. Thanks.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): I'll sort the diclofenac and show you down to CT.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mind yourself, Seán. We'll get this sorted.

spec.situation: Sudden severe loin pain going to the groin overnight, vomiting once, blood in urine; pain score given loosely; urine dip result read aloud; painkiller and scan planned today.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
